```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center")
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
source("R/clean_air_quality.R")

# Process each year separately and then combine the data.
air_2018 <- process_air_quality("data/AQ_2018.csv")
air_2019 <- process_air_quality("data/AQ_2019.csv")
air_2020 <- process_air_quality("data/AQ_2020.csv")
air <- bind_rows(air_2018, air_2019, air_2020)
air$year <- factor(format(air$date, "%Y"), levels = c("2018", "2019", "2020"))
air$month <- factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(air$date, "%m"))], levels = month.abb)

make_table <- function(data) {
  data.frame(
    Pollutant = c("CO (ppm)", "PM2.5 (ug/m3)", "O3 (ppm)"),
    Minimum = sprintf("%.3f", c(min(data$co, na.rm = TRUE),
                                min(data$pm25, na.rm = TRUE),
                                min(data$o3, na.rm = TRUE))),
    Maximum = sprintf("%.3f", c(max(data$co, na.rm = TRUE),
                                max(data$pm25, na.rm = TRUE),
                                max(data$o3, na.rm = TRUE)))
  )
}
```

## Data processing

I removed duplicate rows and changed negative pollutant values to zero before finding the daily means. This matters because doing the steps after averaging could change the daily results. The cleaned dataset has one row per day.

## Daily concentration ranges

```{r table2018}
kable(make_table(air_2018), caption = "Table 1. Daily concentration ranges in 2018", align = "lrr")
```

```{r table2019}
kable(make_table(air_2019), caption = "Table 2. Daily concentration ranges in 2019", align = "lrr")
```

```{r table2020}
kable(make_table(air_2020), caption = "Table 3. Daily concentration ranges in 2020 (January–April)", align = "lrr")
```

## Monthly CO and ozone concentrations

```{r plot1, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 1. Monthly mean concentrations and 95% confidence intervals, using available daily values from 2018–2020."}
monthly <- air %>%
  select(month, co, o3) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(co, o3), names_to = "pollutant", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(month, pollutant) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(value)),
            avg = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            s = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(lower = avg - 1.96 * s / sqrt(n),
         upper = avg + 1.96 * s / sqrt(n),
         pollutant = factor(pollutant, levels = c("co", "o3"),
                            labels = c("CO (ppm)", "Ozone (ppm)")))

ggplot(monthly, aes(x = month, y = avg, color = pollutant)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ pollutant, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("CO (ppm)" = "#246B8F",
                                "Ozone (ppm)" = "#C76A39")) +
  labs(title = "CO and ozone by month", x = "Month",
       y = "Monthly mean concentration", color = "Pollutant") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

I used separate panels because CO and ozone have very different scales. This makes both patterns readable without changing the units.

## Monthly PM2.5 concentrations by year

```{r plot2, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Figure 2. Monthly mean PM2.5 concentrations for each year."}
pm_monthly <- air %>%
  group_by(year, month) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = mean(pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(pm_monthly, aes(x = month, y = pm25, color = year, group = year)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2018" = "#246B8F",
                                "2019" = "#2D8661", "2020" = "#C76A39")) +
  labs(title = "PM2.5 by month and year", x = "Month",
       y = "Monthly mean PM2.5 (ug/m3)", color = "Year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

I used lines and points because they make it easy to compare how PM2.5 changes over the months in each year.

## Interpretation

CO is generally higher in late fall and winter, while ozone is higher in spring and summer. The 2020 table has the largest daily PM2.5 value, but monthly PM2.5 was lower in early 2020 than in early 2018 and 2019. Since the 2020 data only include January through April, we cannot compare the rest of that year.
